title: Infra team wiki: GPU fleet capacity, IaC modules, CI/CD & runbooks
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary:
This page consolidates guidance for the infra team on GPU fleet capacity planning, Terraform/IaC module standards, CI/CD build pipelines for infra modules, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical team wiki entry for everyday decisions and incident response related to the GPU-capacity and related IaC systems.

1) Overview
- Goal: maintain predictable GPU capacity for Redwood’s Hosted and Dedicated fleets while minimizing cost and meeting latency SLOs.
- Scope: fleet sizing, cloud accounts & networking primitives, Terraform module patterns, CI/CD pipelines, and runbooks for capacity incidents and deployments.

2) Owners and escalation
- Primary owner: infra-capacity (team)
- Secondary owners: cloud-accounts, networking, ci-cd, runtime-ops
- Pager rotation: infra-oncall (see team rota)
- Escalation path: oncall -> infra-shift lead -> infra-eng manager -> eng-sre

3) Capacity planning and SLOs
- Target SLOs (for production inference fleet):
  - 99th percentile tail latency: <= 120ms for <1k-token requests (region-dependant)
  - Throughput availability: >= 99.9% (capacity-demand accepted by scheduler)
  - Queue drop rate: < 0.1% under steady state
- Headroom policy: aim for 25% spare capacity vs. 30-day p95 predicted demand; reduce to 15% during cost-constrained months with approval.
- Scaling cadence: weekly demand review, monthly capacity refresh planning, quarterly architecture review for new HW types.

4) GPU fleet: instance types and allocation strategy
- Preferred instance families (ordered): A100-80GB (primary), H100-80GB (high-throughput), A10G (inference-economy), T4 (embeddings/batch).
- Allocation rules:
  1. Match model class to preferred family via runtime-profile mapping table.
  2. Place Dedicated customer workloads into reserved pools first.
  3. Use preemptible/spot capacity for non-SLA interactive workloads and for background batching jobs.
- Example mapping table (text):
  Model class | Preferred family | Notes
  ------------|------------------|------
  Large chat (8k+) | H100-80GB | high throughput, long context
  Multi-turn chat (2k) | A100-80GB | latency-sensitive
  Embeddings / batch | T4/A10G | cost-optimized

5) Cloud accounts & networking notes
- Account boundaries: per-region infra accounts for GPU pools, separate accounts for control plane and customer-dedicated pools.
- VPC design: one primary VPC per region for shared services; isolated VPCs/subnets for dedicated pools with VPC peering or PrivateLink for control-plane access.
- Network security groups: allow only required control-plane ports (SSH: restricted, API: TLS-only 443), internal gRPC ports between nodes, and monitoring agents.
- Egress policies: enforce NAT gateway egress via central logging and egress-limiting CIDR lists.

6) Terraform / IaC modules: standards and patterns
- Principles:
  - Modules are versioned semantically and published to the internal module registry.
  - Keep modules small and focused (networking, compute, autoscaler, iam, monitoring).
  - All modules must include docs/README.md, examples/, and automated unit tests (terraform-compliance / kitchen-terraform).
- Naming conventions:
  - Module name: rf-<domain>-<purpose> (e.g., rf-gpu-pool, rf-network-base).
  - Resource tags: {"team": "infra-capacity", "env": "prod|staging|dev", "service": "gpu-runtime"}
- Inputs/outputs (guidelines):
  - Inputs: accept explicit CIDR blocks, list of instance_types, desired_capacity, min/max, accel_type, and tags; avoid hidden defaults for critical values.
  - Outputs: expose ids (asg/id, instance_profile, subnet_ids) and computed capacity metrics.
- Example module usage (snippet):
  module "gpu_pool" {
    source = "git::ssh://git.internal.company/scm/infra/rf-gpu-pool.git//modules/pool?ref=v1.3.0"
    env = "prod"
    instance_types = ["p4d.24xlarge", "p3dn.24xlarge"]
    desired_capacity = 20
    min_capacity = 10
    max_capacity = 40
  }

7) CI/CD pipeline for infra modules (high level)
- Stages:
  1. Pre-commit/lint: terraform fmt, tflint
  2. Unit tests: terraform-compliance/unit checks in PR CI
  3. Integration plan: run terraform plan against ephemeral test account using terratest or terraform-ci runner
  4. Review and approval: 2 approvers required for prod changes, 1 for staging/dev
  5. Apply: automated apply for non-prod after merge; manual apply via pipeline for prod with gated approvals and canary steps
- Release tagging: tag releases with semantic version (e.g., v1.3.0) and include CHANGELOG.md for breaking changes.
- Secrets: store AWS keys, KMS keys, and provider credentials in Vault; pipelines must use dynamic short-lived credentials.

8) Runbooks and operational playbooks
- Incident triage: GPU capacity pressure (high queueing or dropped requests)
  1. Pager fires to infra-oncall.
  2. Triage: check the capacity dashboard (per-region capacity, autoscaler health, pending requests).
  3. Quick actions (ordered):
     a) Increase autoscaler max_capacity by +25% (if headroom permits) via staging apply to prod-control plane pipeline.
     b) Temporarily reclassify lower-priority workloads to spot pool.
     c) Route traffic to alternate region if cross-region capacity available and model compatibility allows.
     d) If immediate scaling not possible, fallback to a cheaper model variant with graceful degradation.
  4. Post-incident: create incident ticket, populate runbook actions taken, update capacity forecast.
- Routine maintenance: rolling driver updates and kernel patches
  - Schedule: maintenance window: Sun 03:00-07:00 local region time or as agreed with customers for Dedicated pools.
  - Steps: drain nodes from scheduler -> apply updates -> validate runtime health (latency/throughput smoke tests) -> bring nodes back -> monitor for 2h.

9) Playbook: provisioning a new regional GPU pool (step-by-step)
1. Create region account checklist: create cloud account, IAM baseline, centralized logging and monitoring config.
2. Provision VPC and subnets using rf-network-base module (include private subnets for compute).
3. Create GPU pool module instance via rf-gpu-pool with desired_capacity and instance_types.
4. Configure autoscaler and health checks (target CPU/GPU utilization and custom inference queue metrics).
5. Run canary deployment with 5% traffic using routing policy and monitor SLOs for 60 minutes.
6. Promote to full production if canary passes.

10) Metrics, dashboards and alerts (minimum set)
- Dashboards: per-region capacity dashboard, per-pool autoscaler health, model-class latency heatmap, cost-per-token trend.
- Alerts (SRE):
  - Autoscaler failing to scale: P1
  - Queue length above threshold for >5m: P1
  - Node provisioning failures >5% of requested: P2
  - Unexpected instance termination events spike: P2

11) Docs and training
- Every change to modules or runbooks must include a short training note in the team channel and updated README.
- Quarterly runbook drills (game days) to validate scaling and provider failure response.

12) References and related pages
- See also: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026.json
- CI templates: internal repo -> infra-ci/templates/gpu-pool-pipeline.yaml

Appendix: Quick commands
- Terraform fmt and validation:
  terraform fmt -recursive && terraform init && terraform validate
- Run a plan in ephemeral account (example):
  export TF_VAR_region=us-west-2
  ./ci/run-plan.sh --module rf-gpu-pool --env prod
